national.title: Iconic NBC Sports announcer Dan Hicks dies at 64
national.summary: Dan Hicks was the voice of golf, Olympic swimming and Notre Dame football during a 35-year career at NBC Sports.
national.body: Sportscaster Dan Hicks, who was the voice of golf, Olympic swimming and Notre Dame football during a 35-year career at NBC Sports, has died, his family and NBC announced Thursday. He was 64. Hicks died late Wednesday in Connecticut. He died of an acute illness, according to his wife, ESPN broadcaster Hannah Storm. "Our family is heartbroken by the sudden and unexpected passing of Dan," Storm said in a statement posted to social media. "He was a devoted husband of over 30 years, loving father to our three daughters, and cherished friend to so many. His loss is immeasurable. "Dan was truly one of a kind and, quite simply, the person everyone wanted to be around. When he walked into a room, he brought the energy, the laughter and the people together. He was endlessly kind, thoughtful and funny, and he made everyone feel like they mattered."Hicks was best known as the lead announcer for golf, as well as swimming and skiing at the Olympics and Notre Dame football. He joined NBC in 1992 following three years at CNN. "I'm incredibly lucky to stay at one place this long. It takes a lot of things going your way as far as NBC continuing to have the properties that I've been a part of through the years," he said during an Associated Press interview in September. "So lots of variables, lots of things that can happen in your career. But I think I appreciate it more and more the longer it's been." Golf was Hicks' favorite sport. He was on the call for 27 tournament victories by Tiger Woods, including three at the U.S. Open. Hicks was a tower announcer from 1995-99 before taking over as the main voice in 2000."This is a tough one, I mean really tough," his golf broadcast colleague and friend Robert Maltbie told Golf Channel. He called 27 U.S. Opens and 23 U.S. Women's Opens as well as the Ryder Cup, PGA Tour and British Open. "Dan's voice filled our living rooms with his steady narration of countless golf broadcasts, calling some of the game's biggest moments," the PGA Tour said in a statement. "The sound of his voice is woven into our memories of the game, and the warmth he brought to the broadcast was matched only by the kindness he showed those around him." USGA CEO Mike Whan added: "He was a true friend to the game and to the USGA, but more importantly, a wonderful person whose warmth, generosity, and friendship touched everyone fortunate enough to know him." national.title: GOP lawmakers negotiating for Huang to appear before Congress
national.summary: Republicans on Capitol Hill are negotiating for now-resigned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang​ to appear before Congress.
national.body: Washington — Republicans on Capitol Hill are negotiating for now-resigned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to appear before Congress about the scandal that has rocked one of the most important companies in the world, lawmakers said Thursday. "We are in discussions with him right now on a date to come and meet with us," said GOP Rep. John Moolenaar of Michigan, the chairman of the House Select Committee on China. But he added: "If for some reason that were not to happen, all three committees, all three chairs have said we will use our subpoena power."Nvidia, whose chips have fueled the AI boom, announced on Thursday that Huang had stepped down following a scandal over his affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at the company Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.Moolenaar and two other chairs — Reps. Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Rick Crawford of the Intelligence Committee — wrote a letter to Huang on Nov. 4 asking him to appear for a closed-door briefing with all three committees. They said the purpose of the briefing would be to discuss Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset." The lawmakers gave Huang a deadline of Wednesday to respond. Mast and Moolenaar told reporters on Thursday that they received a response. Mast said Huang indicated he's willing to appear. Moolenaar said that Huang's resignation "does change the dynamic" surrounding his potential testimony. Republicans still control Congress until January."I think right now our goal is to get him in as soon as possible, so that we have a full understanding of the facts and get to the bottom of the truth of this situation," Moolenaar said.Huang's resignation from the company he co-founded has not dampened calls from members of Congress for answers about Nvidia's relationship with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that gained access to highly prized chips that are banned from being exported to China. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.Republican Sen. national.body: Five people were shot, including one who died, as a gunman opened fire in and outside a gym in Washington, D.C.'s Logan Circle neighborhood on Thursday morning, police said. The suspect barricaded himself in a unit believed to be his in an apartment building over Logan Circle's Vida Fitness before shooting himself, said Jeffery Carroll, the Interim Chief of Police of the Metropolitan Police Department, at a news conference Thursday morning. Police later confirmed the suspect died on the scene. Carroll said there were five victims, not counting the shooter. One is deceased, one is in critical condition and three have non-life-threatening injuries. The injured victims have been transported to area hospitals, Carroll said. Victims found in multiple locations Carroll said police received a call for the shooting just before 8 a.m. and that authorities responded within 30 seconds. The person who was killed was shot in the gym. Other victims included members of a construction crew across the street and a person in the lobby or alley outside the gym, Carroll said. The suspect is believed to have used a handgun, Carroll said. CBS News national security correspondent Nicole Sganga says it appears the suspect opened fire in and outside Vida Fitness, then retreated into a parking garage and ascended into the apartment building before barricading himself in a unit on the seventh floor. A fire also was set inside the building at some point during the incident, Carroll said. He said sprinklers went off and that the fire has been contained. He said police don't "know for sure" who set the fire, but that authorities "would kind of expect" it was the suspect. Gunshots continued to be heard for the better part of two hours, while officers with the Metro Police Department negotiated with the suspect. Carroll said the suspect fired through the apartment door at police on two occasions. While on the phone with negotiators, the suspect shot himself, Carroll said. After hearing the gunshot, officers forced entry into the apartment, where they found the suspect suffering from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Carroll did not say where the suspect shot himself. national.summary: At least eight people were killed and 18 others were injured​ after a building collapsed in Flatbush, Brooklyn.
national.body: The death toll continues to climb after a Brooklyn building collapsed and an adjacent building was significantly damaged.A three-story, multi-use building on Flatbush Avenue collapsed into a nearby construction site just after 4 p.m. Wednesday, tearing off the side of another building. At least eight people were killed and 18 others were injured as of Thursday morning, according to the FDNY. Six people were found dead at the scene, and two died at the hospital. "We know that this morning they pulled out, I believe a couple of construction workers that were on site last night, which added to the death toll this morning," said Councilwoman Farrah Louis. The structure was fully occupied by residents, and construction workers were in the construction pit performing excavation work at the time of the collapse. Emergency crews worked through the night under floodlights with the help of drones and K-9 units to get through the massive piles of rubble. Video showed dozens of firefighters at the scene Thursday morning searching for additional victims. First responders are also using machinery to excavate debris. Officials are trying to determine what caused the ground to give way. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani called the incident devastating, praising first responders for executing a grueling, high-risk technical operation. "Rescue workers have spent the night searching the site of yesterday's building collapse, working under extremely dangerous conditions to find and save anyone who may still be trapped. I am heartbroken that eight New Yorkers have now lost their lives and at least 17 have been injured, including three firefighters. There are no words for a loss of this magnitude," he said in a post Thursday. Investigators are conducting comprehensive reviews of the conditions at the collapsed building and neighboring construction site. Investigators said developers have active permits for excavation and foundation work associated with a new building project.Records revealed the site had been cited for violations months before the disaster. national.title: U.S. envoys meet with Putin in Moscow on Ukraine talks, then head for Dublin to see Zelenskyy
national.summary: Kushner and Witkoff met with Putin in a meeting that lasted about two hours. They then headed for Dublin for talks with Zelenskyy as the conflict stretches toward the five-year mark.
national.body:
Harriet Morris, Associated Press Harriet Morris, Associated Press

MOSCOW (AP) — U.S. envoys met Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin and then left for Ireland to talk with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as Washington sought new momentum in its peace efforts.

Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also President Donald Trump's son-in-law, brokered talks this week between delegations from Moscow and Kyiv. The meeting in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, brought the first direct discussions between Ukrainian and Russian representatives in nine months as the push for a settlement stalled.

The two days of talks that ended Wednesday produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners, with the exact figure still to be announced.

Kushner and Witkoff met with Putin in a meeting that lasted about two hours. They then headed for Dublin for talks with Zelenskyy as the conflict stretches toward the five-year mark.

Kushner said one of the goals of the meeting with Putin was to get the Russian leader's blessing for European representatives to be part of the talks, which are looking at the continent's broader security arrangements.

The U.S. and Zelenskyy want Europe to appoint a single person to negotiate with Moscow.

national.title: Democrats want to stop Trump's arch, golf course and more. What are their options?
national.summary: As Trump's arch and other projects make their way through the courts, many critics are looking to Congress to stop them. Democrats have a few tools, including funding and oversight.
national.body:
President Trump's efforts to remake Washington, D.C., have dominated his second term, even after his party's resounding midterm defeat.

He started his election week at the scandal-plagued Reflecting Pool and ended it with an order declaring his gilded Oval Office a national monument to "make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space."

That proclamation, like any executive order, could be undone by a future president. But many of Trump's construction projects are changing D.C. in more permanent ways.

Politics Trump aims to leave a physical legacy in D.C., bulldozing norms along the way His administration has already downed hundreds of trees at East Potomac Park and demolished the East Wing of the White House to make space for a ballroom — which he called "the safest place in Washington" as he showed it to reporters the day after the midterms.

Trump has taken a uniquely unilateral approach to construction , packing regulatory commissions with his allies and bypassing Congress entirely. Most of his projects — from the triumphal arch to the Kennedy Center — are now playing out in court .

Critics accuse the Trump administration of skirting federal laws and misleading judges in its effort to progress as quickly as possible before the end of his term.

Politics Judge orders an inquiry into potential DOJ misconduct in Trump's golf course case Democrats have vowed to use their soon-to-be congressional majority to push back on what they describe as Trump's "vanity projects."

When asked about that, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR in an email that "no other president has done more to beautify our Nation's interior than President Trump." He cited park cleanups, the Reflecting Pool and the White House helipad and ballroom as examples, and said Democrats "should work with President Trump to make our nation's capital beautiful again."

national.title: Washington DC shooting leaves one dead and four injured as suspect dies after standoff
national.summary: One victim is in a critical condition and three others have non life-threatening injuries, officials say.
national.body:
One person has been killed and four others injured after a gunman opened fire in Washington DC.

The shooting began on Thursday morning local time inside a gym in an apartment building in the Logan Circle neighbourhood, which is about a mile (1.6km) north of the White House.

Police said the male suspect was "contained" after barricading himself in one of the apartments. They later confirmed he had died.

Of those injured, one is in a critical condition and the others have non-life-threatening injuries.

While the suspect was barricaded, "he did fire through the door at officers at least on two occasions", Jefferey Carroll, the interim chief of the Metropolitan Police Department, said at a news conference.

Negotiators had been on the phone with the suspect when they heard a gunshot and he stopped communicating with them, according to Carroll.

Officers forced their way into the apartment and saw the suspect had what appeared to be a "self-inflicted gunshot wound", he said.

Carroll added that police "believe there was a fire that was set", which has been contained.

national.title: Hegseth awards medal to soldier who reprimanded group near tomb
national.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth awarded a medal to the service member who reprimanded his group for making noise at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier​.
national.body: Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth awarded a medal on Thursday to the service member who reprimanded his group for making noise at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day. Hegseth posted a series of photos on X with the soldier, Specialist Thomas Iglesias, and other members of the unit who guard the tomb at Arlington National Cemetery around the clock. One of the photos showed Hegseth pinning a medal to Iglesias' chest. "We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist," Hegseth wrote. "Carry on Patriots."A Pentagon official said Hegseth "welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard, to the Pentagon where he proudly awarded Specialist Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026."Iglesias was guarding the Tomb following a Veterans Day event that included Hegseth, President Trump and other administration officials. Footage showed Hegseth, his wife, his chief of staff and other aides posing for photos near the tomb. Someone laughed, and Iglesias shouted: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."In the aftermath, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told CBS News: "The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored-and will always honor-the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe. While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."Soldiers reminding visitors to maintain decorum at the tomb is not uncommon. One member of the regiment that guards the tomb said in an Army interview in 2022 that sentinels react to the crowd two or three times per day.

national.title: The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
national.summary: Within days, Huang's status as a seemingly untouchable figure leading the global tech race has crumbled.
national.body:
Jensen Huang, known for sporting a black leather jacket to shareholder events, appeared to have it all. He was courted by leaders in both Washington and Beijing, worshipped by investors and seen as a loyal family man. But a rockstar approach to his personal life has ultimately led to his resignation.

The 63-year-old has been married since 1985, long before the foundation of Nvidia, the company that propelled him to tech stardom.

He is known as a workaholic and a demanding manager, with high standards for those who worked for him, which included his own children, promoted within the company. But he has seen his personal reputation go into free fall this week, undone by romantic entanglements, that throw doubt on his focus and his judgement.

On Thursday he resigned following back-to-back revelations of two affairs. News of the first - a relationship with a businesswoman, alleged to be a Chinese spy - ricocheted around the world, raising eyebrows among investors. It was followed on Wednesday by reports that the tech boss had also had an affair with an Nvidia colleague.

His departure creates uncertainty in the global stock market, which was already knocked-off balance in recent weeks. Nvidia is a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China.

Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.

But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology.

The company, which is still valued at nearly $4 trillion despite recent events, is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.

national.title: While many Americans resist, China embraces AI data center boom
national.summary: Far from the opposition American tech giants face, it's smooth sailing for the Chinese AI firms racing to catch up, and hoping to overtake them.
national.body: Ulanqab, China — Off a major highway on the outskirts of Ulanqab, in the Chinese province of Inner Mongolia, Hereford cows roam through corn fields scouring the ground for any dried up remains of the recent harvest.Hovering over the landscape are shiny new transmission towers linked by power cables that stretch along the plateau for as far as the eye can see. On the ridgeline, covered in snow, wind turbines spin, taking full advantage of the ever-blowing wind. The energy pulsing from the remote Chinese region — a combination of renewables and fossil fuels — will soon power multi-story data centers being constructed on farmland as part of a sprawling AI data center construction boom. The construction site is the size of a small American city. It is the biggest, and fastest growing infrastructure project anywhere in China right now.This corner of Inner Mongolia was famous for generations for growing potatoes. Now, it's fast becoming an AI hub, and Chinese officials hope the expansive, rugged landscape will help power the country's ambition to surpass the U.S. as the global leader in artificial intelligence.Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns in wake of affair, China spy scandalBaletu, a 72-year-old farmer, who has lived here for more than 40 years growing potatoes and corn, said the changes across his local landscape are positive. "It doesn't affect my farmland, not at all," he told CBS News. "It's good for the area."A short drive away, CBS News was able to see what all that wind power will soon be feeding. Trucks, cranes and thousands of workers are taking part in the construction project to create one of the biggest data centers anywhere in the world. We drove miles down new roads with multistory data centers going up on either side. Even from the road it was easy to spot the countless racks that will hold servers, semi-conductor chips and cooling and exhaust fans.There are dozens of data centers being built in Inner Mongolia, more than any other part of the vast nation. The reason they have chosen Ulanqab is because it offers cheap, abundant energy. Fossil fuels are still the main source of power here, but they also use renewables, including wind and solar. Ulanqab is one of the most consistently windy locations in the province. national.body: Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of AI tech giant Nvidia effective immediately following a scandal involving an alleged spy, the company's board of directors announced Thursday.The decision came amid an investigation into Huang's affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect was spying for China. President Trump said this week the FBI is investigating romantic and business ties between Huang and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. The two aren't related. national.body: As President Trump's senior envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner landed Thursday in a snowy Moscow to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said connection issues with the Starlink satellite network were again affecting his country's ability to defend itself from incoming Russian missiles and drones.Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces using Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink network, which was also impacted last month, were again facing a "systemic speed restriction." Ukrainian interceptors, used to shoot down Russian weapons, have been losing their Starshield satellite guidance connection this week if they try to fly faster than about 100 miles per hour. "Unfortunately, our units have been recording significant malfunctions in Starshield's operation over Ukraine's territory for several days now: along the entire front line and in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territory," Zelenskyy said in a social media post. "Ukrainian military personnel have already investigated the circumstances, and these are not random errors but a systemic speed restriction. For us, this primarily means a significant increase in the difficulty of intercepting Russian jet-powered drones."A Ukrainian official confirmed the restrictions to CBS News, saying "the speed limitations as of now are on Ukrainian occupied territories and across the contact line. The contact line is the first line of our defense and the first point for interception of Russian drones. national.title: Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills six Palestinians, health ministry says
national.summary: Witnesses say a missile hit a building containing the surgical wards and intensive care units at Nasser hospital, the largest in southern Gaza.
national.body:
Six people have been killed and about 30 injured in an Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital in the southern Gaza Strip, the Hamas-run health ministry says.

The hospital's director said two missiles hit a building containing surgical wards and intensive care units overnight, but that one of the missiles did not explode.

The health ministry said medical staff, patients and companions were killed, among them surgeon Dr Rizq Abu Shaira. It condemned the attack as a "flagrant violation of international laws and conventions".

The Israeli military said it targeted a commander of Hamas's armed wing and other fighters who had used the hospital as a "headquarters" to plan attacks on its forces.

Hamas said that Israel was spreading "false narratives" in a "blatant attempt to cover up a new war crime".

Under international law, hospitals have a protected status, but they have been repeatedly targeted during the Gaza war.

Israel accuses Hamas, which retains security control of parts of Gaza not occupied by Israeli troops, of cynically exploiting civilian infrastructure. It says the group stores weapons and runs command and control rooms in hospitals, which Hamas denies.

Israel does not allow international news organisations, including the BBC, into Gaza, making it difficult to verify what is happening in the territory.

national.title: Pentagon backs war memorial guard who reprimanded Hegseth's group
national.summary: The defence secretary on Thursday awarded the soldier, Specialist Thomas Iglesias, a Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties.
national.body:
The Pentagon has given its backing to a US Army guard who reprimanded a group that included US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at the Arlington National Cemetery.

A video of the Veterans Day observance event on Wednesday showed Hegseth, his wife, and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

The footage showed the army sentinel on duty stepping towards Hegseth's group and shouting: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement: "While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."

"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored - and will always honor - the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe."

On Thursday, he presented an award to the soldier who reprimanded his group.

Hegseth "welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard to the Pentagon where he proudly awarded Specialist Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026," the Pentagon said in a statement.

In a post on X showing the soldier, Hesgeth said: "We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist."

Michael Comer showed no remorse for attempting to kill his son, Koah, and tried to flee the state, Tyler Douglas, lead investigator for the Lexington County Sheriff's Department, told Judge Gary W. Reinhart. Reinhart approved a public defender for Comer and set a hearing for Dec. 10. Comer, 25, has been charged with attempted murder, burglary and unlawfully placing a child at risk in connection with the disappearance and rescue of Koah, who survived. Comer has been in custody in Lexington County since Monday, when his son was reported missing. An attorney for Comer has not yet been appointed. Koah, who rescuers found after about 24 hours, was released from a hospital Tuesday night, Sheriff Jay Koon said. He is expected to make a full recovery and is with family members, authorities said. John Comer said he'd opened his home to his son and grandson on Monday after Michael Comer said they needed a place to stay. On Wednesday, he showed an Associated Press reporter the small hole on a neighbor's property where rescuers uncovered the child. "I cannot imagine how somebody could come to the point that that would be the right thing to do, or the thing to do at all," John Comer told the AP.Authorities haven't revealed anything about Comer's motive. He was sentenced in October to probation after pleading guilty to domestic violence involving the boy's mother.Koah's parents "have had some situations," the sheriff said. "Children," he said, "sometimes get caught in the middle." Dozens of first responders scoured the countryside for the boy with reddish-blond hair. After a full day of searching, authorities found freshly disturbed soil and heard cries from below, the sheriff said. national.title: Ukraine says military Starlink disrupted again as US envoys meet Putin in Moscow
national.summary: Later on Thursday, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will travel to Dublin to meet Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky.
national.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Ukraine's military is again facing "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv is struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.

It came as US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, a day after the latest talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.

Zelensky told European leaders in Dublin that Ukraine was trying to clear up the Starlink situation with the American side.

But he added "some things" were already clear: "If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going."

Starshield was developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX company for government and military use. Along with Starlink, it has come to play a vital role in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.

A similar issue with connectivity affected the front line in late October and lasted about a week before it was fixed. It remained unclear who had ordered the temporary restrictions on Starlink services at the time, with US officials and SpaceX offering differing explanations.

Zelensky said the current disruption had been ongoing for several days and was "helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine".

Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?

national.title: New federal housing rule could displace thousands, experts warn
national.summary: Since 1995, mixed-status families have been permitted to live together in federally funded housing, but a revised rule changes that.
national.body: Residents of federally funded public housing will be required to show proof of U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status under a new rule published Thursday by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.The measure could displace nearly 80,000 people, including tens of thousands of citizens in mixed-status families, from their homes, according to the Center for Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan research and policy institute. Since 1995, mixed-status families have been permitted to live together in HUD-funded housing as long as federal subsidies covered only eligible household members. The new rule may force these families to decide whether to remain together in nonpublic housing or split up their households."This is tearing apart families and sowing division," said Marie Claire Tran-Leung, director of the Evictions Initiative Project and managing attorney at the National Housing Law Project.The rule's prior status, which allowed mixed-status families to live together, worked well for all parties, Tran-Leung said. Mixed-status households often paid a higher share of rent because their subsidies were prorated, experts say. If those families are forced to leave public housing, HUD will likely face financial shortfalls, Tran-Leung said.About 20,000 mixed-status families, or 80,000 people, could be affected by the rule, CBPP's data shows. About 37,000 of those are children, mostly U.S. citizens, CBPP said.The rule is scheduled to take effect on Dec. 14."President Trump warned that the days of illegal aliens and ineligible noncitizens exploiting government-funded welfare programs would be over," HUD Secretary Scott Turner said in a statement. "It's unacceptable that America's homeless veterans, disabled, elderly, and victims of domestic violence languish on waitlists while illegals and ineligibles scam our system. American taxpayers will no longer foot the bill. Promises made, promises kept."Turner's statement said a recent audit identified nearly 200,000 tenants with incomplete or unverified eligibility status. Currently, HUD-funded housing serves only a quarter of eligible households in need.Families in all 50 states will be affected, with the largest concentration in New York, California and Texas. One victim died in the initial shooting, said Jeffery Carroll, interim chief with the Metropolitan Police Department.

national.title: The SS United States takes its final voyage to the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico
national.summary: A ship bigger than the Titanic is being sunk off the coast of Florida to make an artificial reef.
national.body:
A giant ship sunk off the coast of Florida yesterday—and the coast guard didn't do a thing to stop it.

The SS United States is a retired ocean liner that was deliberately sunk on Wednesday to create the world's largest artificial reef. After hours of slow descent, it finally disappeared beneath the waves at 10 p.m. ET last night. It now rests 180 feet beneath the surface at the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico in an upright position.

Measuring almost 1,000 feet from bow to stern, the giant ship is longer than the Titanic. After it's settled on the ocean floor, the ship's hundreds of rooms, corridors and elevator shafts will become a deep-sea playground for divers, fish and other aquatic life.

This transformation gives the SS United States the opportunity for a second life and a new species of passenger.

Susan Gibbs has mixed feelings about the ship's final voyage to the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico. She chairs the board of the SS United States Conservancy, and her grandfather, William Francis Gibbs, designed the ship more than 70 years ago.

"It's a combination of grief, that I will be saying goodbye to her in her current form, but, gratitude and hope in terms of what she will continue to give to the world," she told Morning Edition

The ocean liner took its maiden voyage in 1952, and it shattered the trans-Atlantic speed record, winning the coveted Blue Riband on her opening sail. It still holds the record more than 60 years later.

In the event of war, the SS United States could have been converted from a luxury liner to a military transport vessel able to carry 14,000 troops for 10,000 miles without refueling, though it was never used for this purpose, according to the SS United States Conservancy.

national.title: D.C. shooting leaves 1 person killed, 4 injured. Gunman dead
national.summary: A gunman opened fire at a gym in Washington, D.C.'s Logan Circle Thursday morning. One person has been confirmed killed and four others injured. The gunman is dead, according to police.
national.body:
Local and federal law enforcement respond to reports of an active shooting on Thursday in Washington. Tom Brenner/AP hide caption

Busy morning crowds in Washington, D.C.'s Logan Circle ran for cover after a gunman opened fire at a local gym, VIDA Fitness, killing at least one person and injuring at least four others.

The gunman left the gym area, entered a nearby apartment building where he barricaded himself. Jeffery W. Carroll, the interim Police Chief of the Metropolitan Police Department, who briefed the public this morning, said at the time of the briefing that the shooter had shot himself.

A police spokeswoman later confirmed to NPR that the gunman died.

The Logan Circle neighborhood sits about one mile north of the White House. The block where the shooting occurred, along 15th Street Northwest, is lined with apartment buildings, a church, coffee shops and restaurants.

Residents around the area described a massive law enforcement presence, including FBI agents and SWAT teams, swarming the area minutes after gunshots rang out. Residents were sent emergency text messages ordering them to remain sheltered in place. That order was lifted at around 11:30 a.m.

The first call for help came in at 8 a.m. from people inside the gym, Carroll said. Officers and other emergency responders were on scene within 30 seconds, he said. Responders found one adult man who was shot inside the gym.

Witnesses on scene told NPR that VIDA requires visitors to tap in to gain access to the fitness area. Carroll told media he believes the gunman was a member.

national.title: Sharp swings for Nvidia and oil prices weigh on Wall Street
national.summary: Nvidia's stock plunged as much as 14% at the start of trading following the resignation of Jensen Huang, its CEO, co-founder and face of the brand.
national.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — Big swings for Nvidia's stock price and oil prices are weighing on Wall Street Thursday, but the U.S. market appears to be absorbing them.

After falling nearly 1% at the start of trading, the S&P 500 quickly pared its drop to 0.4%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 50 points, or 0.1%, as of 10:15 a.m. Eastern time, while the Nasdaq composite was down 0.6% after trimming its early loss of 1.6%.

At the center of the action was Nvidia's stock. It plunged as much as 14% at the start of trading following the resignation of Jensen Huang, its CEO, co-founder and face of the brand. The chip company's stock has been sinking since its board announced an investigation into Huang for a relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese government agent.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

It's a stunning fall for Huang and for Nvidia, which had become Wall Street's most valuable and influential stock because of its central role in the artificial-intelligence boom. Its stock price set a record last month after soaring an astounding 1,722% in four years. That compares with the already healthy gain of nearly 109% for the overall S&P 500 over the same time.

But Nvidia's price dropped 27% from then through Wednesday on worries about whether Huang would remain and how Nvidia would navigate a future without him. Nvidia's board answered the first question Thursday morning, when it said Huang resigned, and it named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as its interim CEO.

The second question remains to be determined. And it looms over the entire market because Nvidia and the broader AI industry have been the main reasons the U.S. stock market has set so many records in recent years.

Nvidia, to be sure, is still selling AI chips at a quick rate regardless of who stands on a stage and talks them up. Nvidia quickly halved its early loss from Thursday, and its stock was most recently down 6.1%.

national.title: U.S. envoys meet with Putin in the Kremlin after Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi
national.summary: Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff went to the Kremlin to brief Russian President Vladimir Putin and are scheduled to fly later to Ireland for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
national.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin, left, greets Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, right, and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff, center, during their meeting at the Senate Palace of the Kremlin, Moscow, Thursday. Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik, Kremlin Pool Photo via AP hide caption

MOSCOW — U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys met Thursday with President Vladimir Putin as Washington sought new momentum in peace efforts after two days of U.S.-mediated negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations.

Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also Trump's son-in-law, brokered the talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. Those were the first direct discussions between representatives of Moscow and Kyiv in nine months as the push for peace stalled.

The two days of talks that ended Wednesday produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners, with the exact figure still to be announced.

Kushner and Witkoff went straight to the Kremlin to brief Putin in a meeting that lasted about two hours and are scheduled to fly to Dublin, Ireland, for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as the conflict stretches toward the five-year mark.

Kushner said that one of the goals of the meeting with Putin was to get the Russian leader's blessing for European representatives to be part of the talks, which are looking at the continent's broader security arrangements.

The U.S. and Zelenskyy want Europe to appoint a single person to negotiate with Moscow.

One of the AI industry's most important figures has resigned amid allegations that he had extramarital affairs with two women - one a suspected Chinese spy and the other a company executive.

Chip-maker Nvidia hired a major law firm earlier this week to investigate CEO Jensen Huang's reported relationship with a woman who was allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset.

Now he has resigned after its stocks plummeted on Wednesday following US media reports about a second alleged affair.

Huang admitted , external earlier this week to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and he apologised for hurting her and their children.

Nvidia stocks plummet in US after CEO Jensen Huang quits in wake of affair with suspected Chinese spy

How was Huang removed? Nvidia's board met on Wednesday evening to decide whether its CEO should remain with the company.

It had 11 directors on its board, including Huang. The firm's CEO could be removed with or without cause by a majority vote of directors.

But that wasn't in the end needed - the board instead announced Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member.

national.title: Millions of Ebola dollars missing with staff unpaid while virus spreads, charity says
national.summary: Medical staff are going unpaid, lack proper training and are struggling with shortages of essential supplies, MSF warns
national.body:
Hundreds of millions of dollars meant to help tackle Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo are not reaching the intended recipients, a medical charity has warned.

A report from Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said that while the outbreak remained "out of control", front-line workers were going unpaid, lacked proper training and were struggling with shortages of essential supplies.

More than 5,400 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.

This makes it the second-most deadly outbreak of the disease ever recorded.

MSF has urged the Congolese government and UN agencies to "strengthen oversight and accountability" to ensure money already disbursed is effectively utilised.

This means "ensuring response personnel are properly trained, paid, equipped, and supported, and directing resources towards areas where needs are greatest", it said.

MSF's warning adds to concerns raised by Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) last month, when it said that $700m (£527m) out of $962m disbursed to organisations implementing Ebola response was unaccounted for.

At the time, Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya said it was too early to describe it as embezzlement, characterising the issue as a major transparency and financial reporting failure.

national.title: Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently?
national.summary: Chief financial officer Colette Kress in in charge of Nvidia for now, but several others are in the frame as potential successors.
national.body:
Nvidia is now facing a scenario few would have considered until very recently - a future without Jensen Huang.

The influential co-founder of the AI chip-making giant resigned on Thursday over reports of extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress is in charge, for now, as the tech giant faces one of its biggest challenges - finding the right person to permanently lead the business that Huang helped create more than three decades ago and turned into one of the world's most valuable companies.

We take a look at which candidates have emerged as potential successors.

Colette Kress has been an industry veteran for more than 30 years, having previously held high positions at tech firms like Cisco and Microsoft.

Kress, who also serves as Nvidia's executive vice-president, has seen the firm's transformation from making chips for video games in the early 1990s to becoming an AI semiconductor powerhouse.

She has "fronted every earnings call" alongside Huang and is a "familiar and trusted voice for the market at a time when it badly needs one," said Josh Gilbert, an analyst at investment firm eToro.

But doing the job permanently could be a different story, said Gilbert, as the firm, known for its edge in technology, could want an engineer in the chair.

national.summary: Raka is the son of former President Joko Widodo. The Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled last month that the documents that Raka submitted regarding his overseas education didn't meet election requirements.
national.body:
Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka leaves the parliament building after submitting his resignation letter in Jakarta, Indonesia, Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. Tatan Syuflana/AP hide caption

JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia's vice president resigned on Thursday as questions grew over his eligibility for the office after recent court rulings disputed his educational credentials.

Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, submitted his resignation to the leadership of the People's Consultative Assembly, the country's highest legislative body, at the parliament building in the capital, Jakarta.

"There will always be political dynamics in public office, that's normal," his father, Widodo, told reporters from his hometown in Solo, adding that he had reminded his son that political positions are temporary.

"We will continue to support President Prabowo's government, especially programs that serve the interests of the broader public," he said, referring to Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto.

The academic credentials investigation was apparently not related to investigations into allegations that top police officials had been involved in wiretapping targeting the president.

national.title: Before Scott Colom, these two men were the last black US senators from Mississippi
national.summary: The Democratic candidate won in a southern state that had not seated a black senator since 1874.
national.body:
After winning a close race in Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom will become the state's first black US senator for more than 150 years, and the third in history.

It is a historic result in the deeply conservative southern state that last sent a Democrat to the US Senate in 1982, and had not seated a black senator since 1875.

Colom follows Hiram Revels, who became the first black person ever to serve in the chamber when he was seated from 1870 to 1871, and Blanche Bruce, whose term ran from 1875 to 1881. Revels and Bruce were both members of the Republican Party.

Revels was chosen as Mississippi's first senator after the Civil War, serving for just over a year and campaigning strongly for racial equality.

A few years later, Bruce, who was born into slavery, became the first black person to serve a full term in the US Senate. He remained in Washington after leaving the chamber and held a role in the Treasury.

Both terms came before the repressive Jim Crow laws began to enforce racial segregation across Mississippi and other southern US states.

A significant factor in Colom's victory was his success in mobilising young people and the state's large black population, who are expected to have turned out in high numbers.

In a victory speech, Colom referenced how Revels, who was a minister and served as a chaplain during the Civil War, gained support for his Senate campaign through his words.

national.body:
A senior leader of Colombia's largest criminal gang, the Gulf Clan, is among eight people killed in an air strike carried out by the country's armed forces, according to President Abelardo de la Espriella.

De la Espriella said he had personally authorised the bombing targeting the Gulf Clan in the province of Antioquia, in north-west Colombia.

He added that Haminton Mosquera, whom he described as a senior member of the crime gang and one of 10 "priority targets" for Colombia's security forces, had been "brought down".

De la Espriella was elected in June after campaigning on a promise to crack down on Colombia's powerful criminal gangs, including by launching air strikes.

In a post on X , external , he said that Mosquera was suspected of having ordered attacks against the security forces, including the murder of a police officer in the municipality of Tarazá last year.

The Gulf Clan has been engaging in criminal activities for decades, mainly trafficking cocaine from Colombia to destinations in the US and Europe but also illegal mining and people smuggling.

The US added it to its list of Foreign Terrorist Organisations (FTOs) last year.

In his post, President de la Espriella said that "the offensive won't stop" and vowed to regain control of areas currently controlled by criminal organisations such as the Gulf Clan.

national.title: Democrat Scott Colom makes history as Mississippi's first black senator since 19th Century
national.summary: In a state Trump won two years ago by 22 points, Colom's victory extends a string of Democratic wins in the Senate.
national.body:
Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, delivering a shock victory for the party in a deeply conservative state that has elected Republicans for decades.

Colom's victory makes him the first black person from Mississippi to be seated in the US Senate since Blanche Bruce served from 1875 to 1881.

Fewer than five thousand votes out of nearly a million counted separated him from his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.

The result means the Democrats will hold 55 seats in the 100-member Senate, with a knife-edge race in Alaska still to be called.

Before Scott Colom, these two men were the last black US senators in Mississippi

Published 3 hours ago Colom, 43, won with 49.2% of the vote. Hyde-Smith, who received 48.7%, congratulated Colom in a video posted on X on Wednesday evening and wished him well.

"While this was not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said.

The contest was not considered to be in play until the final weeks of the campaign, given President Donald Trump won the state in the 2024 election by more than 22 points.

national.title: Suspected bomb hoax threats force fresh evacuations of Italian schools
national.summary: Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.
national.body:
Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.

Some 1,800 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported receiving a similar threat to one that created chaos in Italy on Wednesday - even though no devices have been found anywhere.

The Italian government has advised schools that "in the absence of concrete evidence beyond the simple receipt of a mass email indicating a danger, buildings must not not be evacuated".

Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland received threats on Wednesday, too. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.

On Thursday morning, a bomb alert at a Calais rail station delayed international and national train services in northern France.

The latest incidents follow a series of bomb hoaxes last week against airports and airlines in a number of European countries.

Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.

Wednesday's email threat - sent to 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 Italian state schools - was said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan".

A Coalchester, Conn., man who was located in Chautauqua County, is facing charges tied to making threats to an elementary school in Vermont.

On Tuesday, the Chautauqua County Sheriff's Office was called to assist an out of state police agency in regard to the threats. The Brattleboro Police Department in Brattleboro, Vt., was searching for a subject whom they allege contacted their office and threated to commit acts of violence to a school in their jurisdiction.

Through a joint investigation, it was determined that 32-year-old Jacob D. Cunningham made those threats while in Chautauqua County. Deputies with the Sheriff's Office were able to locate and speak with Cunningham.

Subsequently, Cunningham was taken into custody and charged with making a terroristic threat of mass harm and amking a terroristic threat. There were no specific threats against any schools in Chautauqua County.

Cunningham was transported to the county jail and arraigned through the Centralized Arraignment Process. Cunningham is facing additional charges from the Brattleboro Police Department.

Cunningham was sent to the Chautauqua County Jail on $500,000 bond or $250,000 cash bail.

According to television station WCAX in North Burlington, Vt., the Brattleboro Police Department began investigating a phone call received Tuesday morning from an individual who threatened violence against local elementary schools. Police said at the time that the call came from New York state, though local law enforcement officials didn’t believe on Tuesday that students or staff members are in danger. Police were stationed at schools across the area Tuesday as a precaution, with neighboring school districts also notified of the threat. Schools in the area sheltered in place even though law enforcement didn’t think there was any danger to students or staff.

local.body:
Pictured are the people who were instrumental in the design and completion of the memorial statue to honor military veterans in the town of Hanover.

Town Clerk Elizabeth VanCheri, center, is shown cutting the ribbon to unveil the Hanover Veterans’ Memorial Statue on Wednesday afternoon. Pictured left of VanCheri is Wayne Ashley, whose idea started the process. Pictured right of VanCheri are Supervisor Lou Pelletter and Council members Ed Schintzius and Aimee Rogers.

OBSERVER Photos by Braden Carmen Pictured is the Hanover Veterans’ Memorial Statue unveiled on Wednesday afternoon. The statue features a soaring eagle, meant to represent freedom, carrying a fish in its talons, signifying Lake Erie and its significance to the region.

Many local veterans were in attendance at the dedication of a memorial statue on Wednesday afternoon in Hanover.

HANOVER -- Dating back several years, the town of Hanover has been planning and designing a memorial to honor veterans for all they did to keep our nation free and safe. On Veterans Day, the town's hard work was on full display as the memorial was finally unveiled.

A large crowd gathered outside of the Town Hall on Wednesday afternoon for a ceremony to honor veterans and cut the ribbon on the new memorial. Several speakers took their turn at the microphone stand before the ribbon was cut.

The idea for a veterans' memorial first began with former Town Councilman Wayne Ashley. After he left the board, it was Town Clerk Elizabeth VanCheri who took the idea and ran with it. VanCheri welcomed guests with a prepared speech, stating to the many veterans in the crowd, "This memorial was built for you."

VanCheri thanked all of the veterans in attendance for their courage in serving their country. She said she hopes the memorial can be a place where veterans can visit and "feel gratitude and respect" for their service. For families of fallen service members, VanCheri said she hopes the memorial will be a place of "comfort and remembrance." VanCheri hopes that younger generations will learn the meaning of service, sacrifice, courage, and freedom from visiting the memorial.

local.title: PBS documentary series "Crime and Punishment" features the story of Rochester's Austin Reed
local.summary: Reed was born into Rochester's free Black community in 1823 and was later incarcerated. His memoir describes violence and torture behind bars.
local.body:
A new PBS documentary series premiering Monday, Nov. 16 on WXXI-TV features the story of a Rochester native.

"Crime and Punishment in America" is a four-part series examining criminal justice in America from the colonial era to today.

Austin Reed was a Black man who was born free in Rochester in 1823. But his freedom would not last long. After his father died when he was a young child, Reed became an indentured servant and was later sent to the House of Refuge in New York City.

"Which was essentially a prison for children with a bit of schooling," said Lynn Novick, producer and director of the film series.

Reed eventually returned to Rochester and was in and out of prison for 20 years.

His memoir, "The Adventures of a Haunted Convict," documents his experiences with violence and torture as an incarcerated person in his youth and at Auburn Prison in upstate New York.

"He's really wrestling with what is prison for? Why are we torturing people? How do we reckon with the things we've done wrong in this moment and in these kind of places?" Novick said.

"Crime and Punishment in America" will air on WXXI-TV at 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. beginning Monday and running through Thursday. The entire series will re-air on from 3 to 11 p.m. Saturday, Nov. 21.

local.title: Rochester School for the Deaf alumna debuts first book, 'Siren of the Finger Lakes'
local.summary: The glacially-formed landscape of the Finger Lakes is the home of Kristen Sickler's creation, "The Siren of the Finger Lakes," which is now a book — and her first publication under her imprint, The Siren Current Press.
local.body:
Listen • 1:13 The 11 Finger Lakes have a magnetic pull for deaf author Kristen Sickler.

The glacially-formed landscape is the home of her creation, "The Siren of the Finger Lakes," which is now a book — and her first publication under her imprint, The Siren Current Press.

The story is family-friendly and narrated by 9-year-old Liv, a girl who grows up in the Finger Lakes region and pieces together what it is about this place that holds so much meaning within the land and the waters.

Sickler grew up in the area, graduated from the Rochester School for the Deaf, and now lives in Avon. She said the idea came to her last year on Sept. 30, her birthday and the anniversary of her mother's death nine years before. The book was published exactly one year later.

"There's something about all of that coming together on the same date that I hold incredibly close to my heart," Sicklerwrote in an email. " I genuinely believe my mother has been part of this journey in her own way."

Sickler said she has always loved the mysterious and unknown. But while this story touches those themes, she said it felt familiar from the moment she envisioned it.

"I'm surprised that the story hadn't already been thought of before," Sickler said in American Sign Language, speaking through an interpreter. "I'm like, 'How could I possibly be the first one who could concoct something like this?' It's almost strange."

The book is just 40 pages, accounting for short attention spans, Sickler said, while giving readers a sense of connection to a region that carries special meaning to her.

local.title: Groundbreaking for High Falls State Park to take place next week
local.summary: The first phase of the park will break ground Wednesday, and will focus on the Heritage Walk on the eastern rim of High Falls gorge.
local.body:
The groundbreaking for the first phase of High Falls State Park will take place Wednesday, Nov. 18, officials have confirmed.

The first phase of park construction will be High Falls Terrace, overlooking the eastern edge of the gorge. The core of that project phase is the Heritage Walk and Memorial Wall, dedicated to the stories of those who migrated to the Rochester area, from Irish Americans to the Haudenosaunee nations.

Two public hearings hosted by the state later this month will examine the potential environmental impact of the park. The New York State Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation then will prepare a report that details "potentially significant adverse environmental impacts and reasonable alternatives to be evaluated, and outlines the studies and analyses anticipated to support environmental review."

The planned 85-acre park encompassing the High Falls Gorge would be the first state park in the city of Rochester. Its construction would include the development of about five miles of paved pathways, as well as six overlooks, restrooms, and an assortment of pavilions, playgrounds and other amenities.

Local News From the archive: See the designs for High Falls State Park Brian Sharp “A centerpiece of the updated design is the new Heritage Walk, which will be a memorial centered on immigration and the migration of people to Rochester,” according to a release detailing the first phase. Erik Frisch is commissioner of the city's Department of Neighborhood and Business Development. He said the park will likely be a major draw to a part of the city that formerly only served industrial purposes.

"If other urban state park examples are proof of concept, then you know we can expect hundreds of thousands of new visitors coming into the city, into High Falls, to experience this state park, and literally to experience something that has not been experienced prior to the creation of the park," Frisch said.

Public comments on the project will be given in virtual webinars, set for 11 a.m. Nov. 30 and 6 p.m. Dec. 1. Written comments will be accepted through Dec. 6.

The state's parks department declined an interview for this story, instead offering a written statement. In the statement provided to WXXI News, the process was described as standard protocol for projects like High Falls State Park. The final document is meant to guide the project on "potentially significant adverse environmental impacts," "provide an initial identification of mitigation measures," and "provide the public with an opportunity to participate in the identification of impacts," among other goals.

local.title: CWD found in a Sparta deer
local.summary: New York’s big game hunting season has long offered more than the excitement of pursuing whitetails. For thousands of hunters, it represents an opportunity to put healthy, locally harvested venison in the freezer, helping supplement grocery bills while carrying on a deeply rooted outdoor tradition.
local.body:
New York’s big game hunting season has long offered more than the excitement of pursuing whitetails. For thousands of hunters, it represents an opportunity to put healthy, locally harvested venison in the freezer, helping supplement grocery bills while carrying on a deeply rooted outdoor tradition. One of New York’s biggest selling points for hunters, including those traveling hundreds of miles from other states and Canada, has been its long-standing success in keeping Chronic Wasting Disease out of the wild deer population.

The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation recently confirmed CWD in a wild white-tailed deer harvested in the town of Sparta, Livingston County. It marks the first detection in a wild deer in New York since 2005 and has prompted DEC to activate its CWD Response Plan to determine how widespread the disease may be and take steps to prevent further spread.

The news is certainly concerning, but it is also an opportunity to recognize the tremendous effort that has gone into protecting New York’s deer herd over the past two decades.

CWD first appeared in New York in 2005, when the disease was discovered in captive deer facilities in Oneida County. Subsequent testing identified two infected wild deer nearby. DEC, working with the Department of Agriculture and Markets, launched an intensive response involving testing, containment, and the removal of affected deer. The effort ultimately eliminated that outbreak, making New York a notable success story in CWD management. Since then, tens of thousands of deer have been tested through ongoing surveillance without another positive wild-deer detection until now.

That vigilance matters. In 2025 alone, DEC tested more than 3,000 deer for CWD as part of its statewide monitoring program. Although a captive deer herd in Herkimer County tested positive in 2024, targeted testing did not identify the disease in surrounding wild deer. The Livingston County finding remains the only newly identified positive wild-deer detection in the state.

CWD is a highly contagious, always-fatal disease affecting the brain and nervous system of deer, elk, and moose. While there is no evidence that it can infect humans or domestic livestock, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends against consuming venison from an animal known to have CWD.

For hunters in the newly established containment area, which includes Conesus, Groveland, North Dansville, Sparta, Springwater and West Sparta, additional precautions are now required. All harvested deer must be submitted for tissue sampling, and whole deer cannot be transported outside the containment area without following DEC’s transport requirements. Collection locations and instructions are available through DEC’s CWD information resources.

BUFFALO (AP) -- Nikita Kucherov had a natural hat trick and an assist -- all in the third period -- and the Tampa Bay Lightning beat the Buffalo Sabres 8-3 on Wednesday night for their fourth victory in five games.

Kucherov, the Russian star who requested a trade Oct. 30, had his eighth NHL hat trick after the Sabres scored three in a row to cut it to 4-3.

Brandon Hagel scored twice, John Carlson had a goal and four assists, and Scott Sabourin and Yanni Gourde also scored. Jake Guentzel had four assists, and Anthony Cirelli added three, and Andrei Vasilevskiy made 28 saves.

Josh Doan, Jason Zucker and Tage Thompson scored for the Sabres, who have lost three of their last four. Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen made nine saves on 14 shots and Colten Ellis stopped five of eight shots in relief.

Thompson cut it to 4-3 33 seconds into the third period, but Kucherov soon took over, scoring his first two in a 2:46 span.

local.body:
Milwaukee’s Jacob Misiorowski and the New York Yankees’ Cam Schlittler were unanimous Cy Young Award winners Wednesday night after delivering dominant performances in their first full major league seasons.

Misiorowski, who reached 105.5 mph with his fastball this summer, won the NL award after helping the Brewers win their first World Series title. Schlittler became the second Yankees pitcher in four years to receive the AL award.

The right-handers made their major league debuts in the summer of 2025.

“It’s exciting,” Misiorowski said. “And then you look one year past that and you’ve got (2025 NL Cy Young Award winner) Paul Skenes also doing it in his second year. It’s really cool, the youth that’s coming up in the big leagues. It’s going to be fun to watch for years to come.”

This was the third time both Cy Young winners were unanimous picks by the Baseball Writers’ Association of America. Houston’s Justin Verlander won in the AL in 2022 and Miami’s Sandy Alcantara in the NL, and Detroit’s Denny McLain won in the AL in 1968 and St. Louis’ Bob Gibson in the NL.

“Realistically when you come into your first full season of the year, do you think you’re going to do that? Maybe not,” Schlittler said. “But you also have the confidence that you can do that. I definitely had conversations with guys in spring training, and that’s kind of a minor goal you put for yourself. I’m just glad to live up to the expectations.”

Misiorowski is 24 and Schlittler is 25, making this the fourth time that both Cy Young winners were 25 or younger, according to Sportradar. The other instances were in 1969 (Tom Seaver and McLain), 1985 (Dwight Gooden and Bret Saberhagen) and 2009 (Tim Lincecum and Zack Greinke).

Toronto’s Louis Varland won the BBWAA’s inaugural AL Reliever of the Year award, while San Diego’s Mason Miller was a unanimous selection for the NL version.

local.body:
Halloween 2026 is history, but the spooks are still standing on many front lawns. You know the ones - the 12-foot skeletons that tower over the rhododendrons - and make me anxious, even at this age. At least the bloody ghouls are mostly packed away now.

I never liked Halloween. I know, I know. It's almost unamerican. But it started early and never really went away. I was an outcast on Halloween.

As an only child, and the only girl in an all-boy neighborhood, I never had anyone to trick-or-treat with. The boys certainly didn't want to drag along that "sissy girl."

Back in the day, parents didn't go trick-or-treating with their costumed kids - they stayed home to answer the door and pass out homemade popcorn balls or candied apples. Full-sized candy bars were fairly common, and for a scaredy-cat like me they were the only reason to head out there alone. I was afraid of the dark streets, scared of the thick hedges, frightened of the shadows.

Mom's work schedule didn't allow time for sewing a costume, and store-bought costumes weren't big back then. The closest she came to actually making a custom costume for me was cutting up an old sheet to transform me into Casper the Friendly Ghost. A few days ahead of spook night, she surrendered an old sheet to the task.

I remember she dropped the middle of the sheet over my head to cut it to ankle length. "Hold still," she said, "I have to get this even all the way around." She felt for my nose bump so she could locate my eyes. "Don't move until I outline them both." Then she removed the sheet to cut out the eyeholes. "There, you're ready to scare everybody out of their best candy bars."

It wasn't easy keeping the crooked eyeholes lined up on Halloween night. I worked hard at not tripping up and down porch stairs and hanging on to my brown paper shopping bag. I wore "Casper" for three years. When the sheet was approaching knee length, it was time to retire the ghost. The next easiest costume? A witch, of course. And Mom was home that Halloween.

I was in the fourth or fifth grade when she jury-rigged the witch's hat for me. She had a pretty, large-brimmed black picture hat. With pieces of black construction paper, she fashioned a pointed cone that she pinned over the hat's crown. Adding an old black coat of hers that dragged on the ground after I was buttoned in, she declared me a wonderful witch. "But they can see my face," I complained. She then drew heavy dark circles around my eyes with her mascara. It was quite a transformation. I looked both scary and half dead - and not much like myself. I went out alone. Again. I always walked tense, fearful, and that year I struggled with the too-long coat, dragging it over the curbstones.

local.body:
JAMESTOWN -- It's already been a dream season for the Jamestown Community College women’s soccer team as they prepare for the NJCAA Division III Tournament.

"It's been crazy. It's been incredible," said sophomore goalkeeper Angel Busch. "I don't think anyone thought this was possible. Our goal was to win five games, and we've made it this far. It is pretty great."

The Jayhawks won their fifth game of the season Sept. 19 to improve to 5-0-0.

"I think a lot of us went into this season looking at it as a stepping stone year to eventually get here, but no one thought it would happen this quickly," said freshman midfielder Gracie Chimera.

Crazy, maybe. Historic for JCC, absolutely. The Jayhawks' 12 wins are a program record, and this squad is on pace to set a team-high for goals scored per game and the fewest goals allowed in a season. Most importantly, they're the first JCC women's soccer team to win a regional championship and advance to nationals.

"I think it is literally crazy," said sophomore forward Sarah Kruszka. "I don't have any other words for it. Seeing the banner in the gym, and it was empty, and now we're the first year to put it up there. That is something I'll tell my kids about. We did that."

"We have always joked that we will be the first team on the banner, and now we made it true," said freshman defender Kennady Ellsworth. "This has been one of my favorite years playing soccer ever."

All the accolades are deserved, but it begs the question: How did the Jayhawks flip the switch so quickly? The players point to their first-year head coach, Sarah Chimera, who brought together a collection of familiar talent she has known and coached for years throughout the Jamestown region.

local.summary: As the city begins paving over some of those historic brick roads, residents are weighing the loss of a familiar piece of their neighborhood against the need for safer, smoother streets.
local.body: For generations, brick streets have been part of the landscape on Buffalo's East Side. But as the city begins paving over some of those historic roads, residents are weighing the loss of a familiar piece of their neighborhood against the need for safer, smoother streets.On Daisy Place, the change has been welcomed by residents who say the uneven bricks had become difficult to navigate, both for drivers and pedestrians.Ken Lee, who has lived on Daisy Place for about 25 years, said the condition of the road had become a problem for drivers."I think it is a beautiful thing because I have been on this street for about 25 years, and this street was terrible," Lee said. "Cars, you could hear them bottoming out when they go here. It was like having its own speed bump."Lee said drivers often had to maneuver around deep divots in the road."You would have to almost go on the sidewalk to escape the divots," he said.Billy Banks, who has also lived on Daisy Place for more than 20 years, shared photos showing the road's condition before it was paved. She said the deteriorating surface made walking difficult and raised concerns about potential injuries."Right now, I feel better because, again, I'm not going to damage my vehicle," Banks said. "Pedestrians aren't going to get hurt by stepping in a sinkhole, basically, and aesthetically, it looks great."WATCH: Buffalo's historic brick roads spark mixed feelings as city paves over East Side streetsBut just nearby on Viola Park, the historic brick roadway remains. Some residents there say they would welcome the same improvements.Madino Osman, who lives on Viola Park, said the uneven road has made getting around more difficult, particularly when walking with children or family members.She said paving the road would make it easier to take her children to the bus and help family members avoid discomfort from the bumps.The city said its Department of Public Works sent postcards to residents asking whether they had any objections to paving the road. According to the city, no residents voted in opposition.The area's councilmember also requested the paving, citing the road's dangerous condition.While the bricks are no longer visible on Daisy Place, the city says they remain intact beneath the pavement and could potentially be restored in the future. local.title: 'Hot dogs don't cost $12'
local.summary: The “street pricing” bill would limit what certain taxpayer-subsidized venues can charge for food and drinks. The effort comes as Buffalo Bills fans face some of the NFL’s highest concession prices.
local.body: The cost of attending a Buffalo Bills game is among the most expensive in the NFL, in large part due to the team's success on the field, which pushes up the price of tickets. But you'll also be digging deep into your pockets once you get through the gates.State lawmakers are scrutinizing the price of food and drinks inside Highmark Stadium and other venues that are subsidized by taxpayers.The issue was the focus of a hearing before the Assembly Committee on Consumer Affairs and Protection. Consumer advocates and other experts pushed for legislation that would limit some concession prices.Brian Hess, executive director of the nonprofit Sports Fans Coalition, testified at the hearing. He pointed to Highmark Stadium as an example of the problem, saying it sells the most expensive hot dog in the NFL at $11.63."Hot dogs don't cost $12," Hess said. entertainment.title: British actress’s Columbia University student daughter dies at 27
entertainment.summary: Lisa Maxwell's daughter, Beau Jessup, was studying journalism at Columbia University in NYC when she died at the age of 27.
entertainment.body:
“The Bill” alum Lisa Maxwell’s daughter, Beau Jessup, has died. She was 27.

Columbia University in New York City announced the M.S. Journalism student’s unexpected death via Instagram Wednesday.

“We extend our deepest condolences to her family, friends, classmates and all who knew and loved her,” a separate statement read.

While the Ivy League school didn’t disclose Jessup’s cause of death, it released an unpublished interview with Jessup from last month, which was conducted as part of its “Notebook” series.

According to the university, the college student was drawn toward “cultural journalism, particularly how institutions, identity, and social expectations influence the way we live and understand one another.”

Jessup told the publication her interest in reporting was sparked during her studies of social anthropology and writing for performance at the London School of Economics and the University of Cambridge, respectively.

She was six months shy of graduating with her master’s degree in May 2027.

In the interview, Jessup also reflected on growing up in a famous household with her mom, a “Loose Women” panelist, explaining, “As the daughter of a television actress, I grew up with an unusual awareness of the distance between people’s lives and the stories told about them.”

And the dress was the cherry, or love, on top of an otherwise perfect day.

Logo text For once, nobody can accuse Charlotte Kirk of going off-script. There wasn’t one.

The British actress, 34, has been keeping busy with monster movies and gangster thrillers since she started making headlines in 2019, when her entanglements with Kevin Tsujihara and Ron Meyer helped topple both studio chiefs. Now she’s dabbling in a much more festive genre, starring in Christmas & Chaos , a holiday film directed by Jamie Adams, the British indie maverick known for shooting entirely improvised films.

“He’d write a few things in the morning — like, this is what we could do,” explains Kirk. “But we just went off on our own. We’d do a take that lasted 40 minutes. By the end, we had 30 hours of footage, enough for four movies.” Related Stories Business Small World: Ron Meyer Had a Fling with Charlotte Kirk's Manager, Too Movies Charlotte Kirk's 'The Reckoning' Sells to RLJE Films, Shudder

In the edit they ended up with, Kirk plays a washed-up pop star who gets paired with her polar opposite, a stubborn music purist (Welsh actor Ben McGregor), to write Christmas tunes. If that sounds like the setup for a meet-cute rom-com, don’t get your hopes up. “I actually do have a romance in the movie,” Kirk tells Rambling, “just with somebody else.”

The film was released Nov. 9 in the U.K., with U.S. distribution still in the works. But Kirk does report one promising development: “We got an airline deal,” she says. Which airline? “I don’t know,” she admits. “My sales agent just said we got an airline deal. I’m like, ‘OK, great.’ “
